teach.title: Feet: the dactyl and the spondee
teach.say: Latin verse has no rhyme. What makes it verse is **the metre (the rhythm of a line: the hexameter and pentameter of the elegiac couplet, Catullus's eleven-syllable line)** — a fixed run of long and short syllables. The syllables come in groups called feet, and two matter here: the dactyl, one long and two shorts (– ⏑ ⏑), and the spondee, two longs (– –). Two shorts take about as long to say as one long, which is why either may stand in for the other. Feet are counted in syllables, not in words, so a foot can stop in the middle of a word.

check.ask: Tap the word that the first foot cuts in half.

teach.title: The hexameter: six feet
teach.say: The commonest line is the hexameter — Greek *hex*, six — six feet in a row. The first four may each be a dactyl or a spondee as the poet pleases; the fifth is almost always a dactyl; the sixth has only two syllables. That is what gives every hexameter its unmistakable falling close, *– ⏑ ⏑ | – –*.

check.ask: Four spondees open this line. Tap the word that fills the fourth of them exactly, by itself.

teach.title: The pentameter, and the couplet
teach.say: Under every hexameter of Ovid and Martial stands a shorter line, the pentameter — Greek *pente*, five, because its two halves of two and a half feet come to five. The first half may take spondees; the second half never does, and is always *– ⏑ ⏑ | – ⏑ ⏑ | –*. A clear break, the caesura, falls between the halves. Hexameter then pentameter is the elegiac couplet: ec-01 and ec-02 are one.

check.ask: Tap the word that opens the second half, straight after the break.

teach.title: Catullus's eleven-syllable line
teach.say: Catullus often counts syllables instead of six feet. The hendecasyllable — Greek *hendeka*, eleven — has exactly eleven, shaped *– – | – ⏑ ⏑ | – ⏑ | – ⏑ | – ⏓*: one dactyl, early, then an even tramp. Martial writes both this and the couplet, so count the syllables of a poem's first line before you start dividing it into feet.

check.ask: Tap the only dactyl in this line — the one word that is long, short, short.

core.text: Latin verse runs not on rhyme but on **the metre (the rhythm of a line: the hexameter and pentameter of the elegiac couplet, Catullus's eleven-syllable line)** — a fixed pattern of long (–) and short (⏑) syllables (the prosody lesson says which). Syllables group into feet: a dactyl (– ⏑ ⏑, *fē-mi-na*) or a spondee (– –, *nē-mō*). Latin name: *versus: hexameter, pentameter, hendecasyllabus*.
Like *DUM-da-da DUM-da-da* in a limerick: the beat is the pattern, the words must fit it. 'Long' means takes longer to say, not louder.

Hexameter: six feet of dactyls or spondees, fifth nearly always a dactyl, sixth two syllables. Pentameter: two halves of two and a half feet with a break (||), the second half always dactyl, dactyl, syllable. Hexameter + pentameter = elegiac couplet.

invented.la: Sīc nautae currunt, sīc ventus flāmina mittit.
invented.en: So the sailors run, so the wind sends its blasts. (a made-up hexameter: – – | – – | – – | – – | – ⏑ ⏑ | – –)

core.text: Ovid (Week 13): *Nōn ego | nōbili|um sede|ō studi|ōsus e|quōrum* — five dactyls, spondee; *cui tamen | ipsa fa|vēs || vincat ut | ille pre|cor* — dactyl, dactyl, half, twice. *um* is long before *s*; *sus* stays short.
Metre is the pattern to fill; prosody is the rules for syllable length and swallowed vowels. Mark syllables first, then divide into feet.

more.text: Martial's couplet (Week 14) scanned: *Nōn amo | tē, Sabi|dī, nec | possum | dīcere | quārē* — dactyl, dactyl, spondee, spondee, dactyl, spondee; *Hoc tan|tum pos|sum || dīcere | nōn amo | tē* — spondee, spondee, half; dactyl, dactyl, half. Twice the final *-ō* of *amō* is counted short, a licence Ørberg notes (*volŏ, nēmŏ*); *nec* and *Hoc* are long because a consonant follows.

Ørberg's chapter 34 (*Dē versibus*) explains the names: the hexameter from Greek *hex*, six, because it has six feet, five dactyls (spondees may replace them, but the fifth is almost always a dactyl — a spondaic fifth foot is a rare special effect) and a final spondee or trochee (– ⏑); the pentameter from *pente*, five, because its two halves of two and a half feet make five, and the second half admits no spondees; a pentameter always follows a hexameter. The break in the middle of a pentameter, and the word-break usually found in the third foot of a hexameter (*Nōn amō tē, Sabidī, || nec possum*), is the caesura, the natural pause when reading aloud.

Catullus's hendecasyllable (Greek *hendeka*, eleven) has eleven syllables in five feet: spondee, dactyl, trochee, trochee, spondee or trochee — *Vīvā|mus mea | Lesbi(a) | atqu(e) a|mēmus*; *Passer | mortuus | est me|ae pu|ellae*; *Cēnā|bis bene | mī Fa|bull(e) a|pud mē*. Its first foot is occasionally an iamb (⏑ –) or a trochee. Ovid wrote the *Amōrēs* in couplets; Martial's epigrams use both the couplet and the hendecasyllable.

sources: Ørberg cap. XXXIV Grammatica Latina (Dē versibus)
